text.hook:
"A string copy shares the buffer until someone writes."
That answer stopped being true in C++11.

The std::string mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Swipe ➜ and save it.
text.body:
Inside:
1. The object vs the characters
2. SSO, library by library
3. Which calls kill your pointers
4. Capacity and construction traps
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: SSO, capacity, which calls kill your pointers, and the construction traps.

slides.title: Two places to keep apart

cards.label: The object
cards.text: Pointer, size, capacity. Lives where you declared it: stack, heap, a member.

cards.label: The characters
cards.text: Inside the object for short strings (SSO), else in a heap block it owns.

cards.label: Borrows
cards.text: Pointers, iterators, `string_view`: the string decides when they die.

slides.takeaway: A copy copies the characters. No sharing since C++11.

slides.title: Small string optimization (64-bit)
slides.takeaway: The standard does not require SSO. libstdc++ row verified with GCC 11, x86-64; the others are typical values.

slides.title: Does it invalidate `p = s.c_str()`?
slides.takeaway: Stricter than `std::vector`. Reacquire, or store an index.

slides.lead: With SSO the characters sit inside the object, so a move or `swap` copies them. That is why both invalidate pointers into a string, while `vector::swap` keeps them valid.

slides.title: What each call really changes
rows: capacity ≥ n, size unchanged; never shrinks (C++20)
slides.takeaway: Growth is geometric: libstdc++ doubles (15, 30, 60, 120), MSVC typically grows 1.5x.

slides.title: Compiles. Not what you meant.
rows: `"llo"`: 2 is a position. From `"hello"` (a `const char*`) it is a count: `"he"`
slides.takeaway: Braces pick `initializer_list<char>` whenever they can. Use parentheses for a count and a char.

items.myth: "Copies share the buffer until one is modified."
items.truth: Copy-on-write is forbidden since C++11. Every copy owns its characters.
Size becomes 0, capacity is kept. `shrink_to_fit` is only a request.
It returns an empty string. Only `pos > size()` throws.

items.myth: "`+=` within capacity keeps my `c_str()` pointer valid."
items.truth: Any non-const member except the access functions formally invalidates it.
Since C++11 both return the same null-terminated pointer.

slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
`if (text.find("key"))` reads like "contains".
It passed code review.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Two `if`s and one comparison. Three characters of output.

slides.title: What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: `find` returns a position, not a bool
bullets: `"key"` is found at position **0**, which converts to `false`: prints `B`.
`"zzz"` is not found: `find` returns `npos` (`size_t(-1)`), non-zero, so `true`: prints `C`.
The truth test is inverted for position 0 and wrong for "not found".

slides.title: Compare with `npos`, or say `contains`
slides.tip: `int pos = s.find(...)` narrows `npos` to `-1`. Keep positions in `std::size_t` or `auto`.

text.hook:
One `reserve(100)` on a 5-char string.
Then the old `c_str()` pointer is printed.
ASan runs clean.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Results: libstdc++ / GCC 11, x86-64. Short strings live somewhere unusual.

slides.title: What happens?

slides.verdict_sub: libstdc++ / GCC 11, x86-64. ASan reports nothing
bullets: `reserve` is a non-const member that is not exempt: `p` is invalidated. Printing it is UB.
`"Hello"` was inline (SSO): `p` points into the string object's 16-byte local buffer.
After `reserve(100)` the chars move to the heap and those bytes hold the capacity: 100 = `0x64` = `'d'`.
Nothing was freed, so ASan stays silent.
slides.wrong: "Prints `[Hello]`: the old characters are still there"

slides.title: Acquire the pointer after the last mutation
slides.tip: Same bug with a 40-char string: the old heap block is freed and ASan reports `heap-use-after-free`.
slides.takeaway: Follow the invalidation rule, not the tool.

text.hook:
"Config value missing? Pass nullptr.
std::string makes it an empty string."
A review comment. True in C++20?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: C++23 changed half of this story. Slide 3 shows which half.

slides.title:
Built with `-std=c++20`.
What happens?

slides.verdict: C. Compiles, UB at run time
bullets: Before C++23, `nullptr` converts to `const char*` and picks the C-string constructor.
That constructor calls `strlen` on a null pointer: UB.
libstdc++ happens to check and throw; other libraries may simply crash.
slides.wrong: "Prints 0: a null pointer is an empty string"

slides.title: The literal is fixed. The runtime null is not.
slides.tip: C++23 adds `basic_string(std::nullptr_t) = delete` (verified with GCC 13). It also rejects `std::string s = 0;`.
slides.takeaway: A null `const char*` is not an empty string. Check it before constructing.

text.hook:
Same 5 bytes: `"ab\0cd"`.
Two strings, three sizes printed.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Binary data in a `std::string` is legal. The question is who is counting.

slides.title: What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: Size depends on who counts: the string or `'\0'`
bullets: `a("ab\0cd")` uses the `const char*` constructor, which finds the length with `strlen`: size 2.
The `s` literal (C++14) receives the array length: all 5 characters, size 5.
`strlen(b.c_str())` stops at the first `'\0'`: 2, although `b.size()` is 5.

slides.title: Keep the length, and never ask C
slides.code:
std::string b = "ab\0cd"s;   // size 5
std::string c("ab\0cd", 5);  // size 5

std::strlen(c.c_str());       // still 2
std::fwrite(c.data(), 1, c.size(), out);
slides.tip: Binary payloads belong in a `std::string` only if they never reach `const char*` C functions.
slides.takeaway: `std::string` tracks its size. C APIs track a terminator.
